name: Straw drinking for coffee

lead: This habit means drinking coffee or other dark drinks through a straw so less liquid reaches the visible surfaces of the teeth, keeping them from yellowing over time. Whitening and appearance communities discuss it as a low-effort preventive habit.

Dental references list frequent consumption of coffee, tea, red wine and cola as causes of extrinsic stain, linked to tannins and other pigments. The idea is reduced contact time between pigmented drink and the front teeth. No study of straw use and staining was found.

paras: People use a reusable or paper straw with iced coffee, tea or other dark drinks and aim it toward the back of the mouth. It is a daily habit that costs nothing and sits alongside brushing and professional cleanings.
No harms are documented, and the effect on stain has not been measured.

angle.text: Whitening communities suggest sipping coffee or dark drinks through a straw so less liquid touches the front teeth and less stain builds up over time. It is a low-effort daily habit that protects a whitened smile. Its effect on stain has not been measured.

lead: Straw drinking for coffee is the habit of sipping coffee, tea or other dark drinks through a straw so that less of the liquid washes over the front teeth. People do it to keep their smile whiter and to slow the yellow-brown surface staining that frequent coffee drinking can cause, and it is discussed as a low-effort habit that sits alongside whitening toothpaste and professional cleaning in smile-care routines [1][2].

Dental references list frequent intake of coffee, tea, red wine and cola as causes of extrinsic stain, which sits on the tooth surface; tannins and similar pigments in these drinks act as chromogens that can stain enamel brown [1][2]. Wikipedia notes that most extrinsic stains are readily removed by cleaning, at home with abrasive whitening toothpaste or professionally by scaling and polishing, and that preventing future stains involves identifying the cause [2].

The straw itself is an old tool: Wikipedia traces drinking tubes to Sumerian beer drinking and the patented paper straw to Marvin Stone in 1888 [3]. No study has measured whether straw use changes tooth staining from coffee.

paras: Proponents use reusable or disposable straws with hot or iced coffee, arguing the drink bypasses the visible surfaces of the front teeth. How far liquid still contacts teeth while it is swallowed has not been measured. Straws come in plastic, paper, glass, silicone and metal; Wikipedia notes that metal straws can damage teeth and that straw use may not always be advisable depending on health circumstances [3].

Tannins in coffee and tea act as chromogens, and heavy consumption can stain enamel brown [1]. Wikipedia's article on tooth discoloration names tea, coffee, red wine and cola as common dietary causes, and notes that chlorhexidine mouthwash can bind tannins and add removable staining when used alongside such drinks [2]. Extrinsic stains lie on the tooth surface; intrinsic stains form within the tooth from causes such as ageing, trauma or fluorosis [1]. Plaque and tobacco also affect staining [2].
Treatment of extrinsic stain includes whitening toothpaste or professional scaling and polishing, and professional whitening uses peroxide-based gels [1][2].

Straws have a long history, from Sumerian beer-drinking tubes to Marvin Stone's 1888 paper straw and the plastic straws that spread after the Second World War [3]. Plastic straws have been restricted in a number of places, including a European Union directive effective July 2021 and a ban in England from October 2020 [3], which has increased interest in reusable alternatives.

No studies found on straw use and tooth staining. Laboratory work on beverage staining exists for related materials, such as a 2025 in vitro study of colour stability of clear aligners exposed to beverages.

timeline.event: Marvin C. Stone patents a paper drinking straw.[3]
